topline: Five stories today: US envoys say Putin will let Europeans into the next round of Ukraine talks, Macron tells the Dublin EPC summit that US support for Kyiv is gone, Merz's threat to tie the EU budget to Ukraine aid shadows today's informal EU summit, Burnham pitches a 'win-win' UK–EU deal a week before their summit, and waves of hoax bomb emails hit thousands of Italian, Irish and UK schools.

stories.title: US envoys say Putin will accept Europeans at the next round of Ukraine peace talks
stories.summary: After meeting Vladimir Putin in Moscow, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner flew to Ireland and met Volodymyr Zelensky at Casement Aerodrome near Dublin on Thursday, on the margins of the European Political Community summit. Witkoff said Putin had agreed that European representatives could join the next negotiating round, though no countries, format or date were named, and Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov did not confirm it. Zelensky said Europe would be on the negotiating team next time and that a coming prisoner exchange, agreed in principle in Abu Dhabi, would be the largest yet. Putin also floated a joint humanitarian mission to front-line Kostiantynivka, while Kyiv complained that SpaceX's Starshield service had again been restricted over Ukraine.
stories.why: For months the EU has argued that no settlement affecting European security can be negotiated without it; a seat at the table would test whether the 27 can agree on who speaks for them.

left.angle: Centre-left coverage paired the envoys' announcement with reasons for caution, putting the renewed Starshield restrictions and Moscow's unchanged demands alongside the diplomatic opening. The European inclusion is treated as a claim still to be proven rather than a breakthrough.

outlets.name: CNN
outlets.note: Headline links the Witkoff–Kushner meeting with Zelensky to Kyiv's complaint that Starshield was restricted again.

right.angle: Right-leaning US coverage led with Witkoff's claim as a sign of momentum for the Trump administration's diplomacy, with European scepticism and the lack of detail placed further down.

outlets.name: Newsmax
outlets.note: Leads on Witkoff calling European participation a big deal; a European diplomat's view of 'maximalist' Russian demands comes later.

stories.differ: The left-leaning take foregrounds friction with Washington (Starshield) and Russian hard lines; the right-leaning take foregrounds the envoys' progress claim.

stories.title: At the Dublin EPC summit, Macron says US support for Ukraine is gone and Europe must lead
stories.summary: About 50 leaders met in Dublin on Thursday for the ninth European Political Community summit, hosted by Taoiseach Micheál Martin. Emmanuel Macron said there was no more US support for Ukraine and that the countries in the room provide roughly 80–90% of the Coalition of the Willing's contribution. Zelensky warned that Russia wants to rewrite Europe's security architecture before any ceasefire, called a US idea of a new security order with Russia 'a bit strange', and asked for interceptors, F-16 ammunition and the opening of the last EU accession clusters this year. Martin listed Ukraine, hybrid threats, technology and affordable energy as the summit's focus and said the EU needs a clear voice at the negotiating table; EU leaders begin discussing a possible EU envoy at today's informal summit.
stories.why: The EPC is turning into a venue where Europe tries to organise its own security response; whether the EU names a single negotiator is the next practical test.

left.angle: Centre-left coverage focused on the show of European unity around Zelensky and on the EU's internal argument over who should represent it. The emphasis is on Europe stepping up, with less attention to what the summit concretely produced.

outlets.name: Channel 4 News
outlets.note: Picture-led piece on UK PM Andy Burnham embracing Zelensky and pledging support in negotiations.

outlets.name: EUobserver
outlets.note: Preview stressing intra-EU splits over an EU envoy and how Ukraine pushed AI down the agenda.

right.angle: We found no right-leaning outlet's own coverage of the Dublin summit or of Macron's remarks in the last 24–36 hours.

stories.differ: Only centre-left and straight-news framings were found: they present the summit as Europe rallying while Washington steps back.

stories.title: Merz's threat to tie the EU budget to Ukraine aid hangs over today's Dublin leaders' meeting
stories.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has written to European Council President António Costa saying Berlin will not back the 2028–2034 EU budget unless all member states commit to closing Ukraine's roughly €70bn funding gap for 2027. Brussels has pledged about €45bn of that through an instrument not yet defined, with joint borrowing the frontrunner; the proposed budget already earmarks €100bn for Ukraine, but only from 2028. Slovakia's Robert Fico called the demand blackmail, and Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria also rejected the link. Costa replied that Ukraine will be discussed at today's informal summit in Dublin, which is formally devoted to AI, and that 2027 financing will be settled at a special summit on 26–27 November.
stories.why: Both the long-term budget and new Ukraine money need unanimity, so a stand-off between Berlin and the central European holdouts could stall both.

left.angle: Centre-left coverage led with Fico's blackmail accusation and the risk that the dispute leaves Ukraine short of money, while noting talk of moving to majority voting to get around vetoes.

outlets.name: The Guardian
outlets.note: Frames the row through the Slovak PM's accusation and Kyiv's funding gap.

right.angle: Right-leaning coverage split: German centre-right press reported the clash straight, while central European conservative outlets cast Fico and Babiš as defending national sovereignty against German pressure.

outlets.name: Die Welt
outlets.note: Leads with the Slovak premier accusing Merz of 'blackmail'.

outlets.name: Hungarian Conservative
outlets.note: Presents Fico and Babiš as pushing back on Berlin and widens the story to V4 objections on climate policy.

stories.differ: The left-leaning piece worries about Ukraine's cash and EU vetoes; the conservative central European piece treats Merz's letter as an overreach against member states.

stories.title: Burnham says a 'win-win' UK–EU deal is possible a week before the bilateral summit
stories.summary: Meeting Ursula von der Leyen on the margins of the Dublin summit, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a mutually beneficial deal could be reached before the UK–EU summit due in about a week, while admitting no agreement exists yet. The package under negotiation covers food and farming (an SPS deal), linking emissions trading systems and a youth mobility scheme. Reports say the EU wants EU students to pay domestic tuition fees in the UK as part of the deal; Burnham called it a package without saying whether he accepts that link. A later phase could cover migration, with London seeking access to EU databases such as Eurodac and the Schengen Information System.
stories.why: It would be the most substantial UK–EU agreement since Brexit, with trade, carbon-market and mobility consequences on both sides of the Channel.

left.angle: Centre-left coverage led with Burnham's optimism and treated the reset as overdue, presenting the tuition-fee demand as the main remaining obstacle.

outlets.name: The Guardian
outlets.note: Burnham's 'win-win' pitch, with the fees dispute and migration-database asks as next hurdles.

right.angle: Right-leaning British coverage focused on sovereignty costs, highlighting peers' warnings that the UK would be absorbing EU rules at speed and Burnham's push to land youth mobility before Christmas.

outlets.name: GB News
outlets.note: Headline relays peers' warning that Britain would adopt EU law 'every 12 hours'.

outlets.name: GB News
outlets.note: Frames the youth mobility scheme as Burnham pushing ahead with a 'Brexit reset'.

stories.differ: The left sees a pragmatic deal within reach; the right sees rule-taking and free-movement creep.

stories.title: Hoax bomb emails hit thousands of schools in Italy, Ireland and the UK
stories.summary: Some 6,300 Italian schools received emailed bomb threats on Wednesday and more than 1,800 more on Thursday, prompting evacuations and closures; police found nothing to substantiate them. Hundreds of schools in Ireland, Scotland and Northern Ireland got similar emails, which authorities classed as hoaxes, and Irish newsrooms and RTÉ were also targeted. The messages were signed by a fictitious 'Mikhail Andropov'. Giorgia Meloni's government said buildings should not be evacuated on the strength of a mass email alone and called it a strategy to spread alarm, while officials in several countries pointed to wider hybrid-warfare concerns without attributing blame.
stories.why: The waves coincide with the Dublin summits and a broader rise in suspected Russian and Iranian hybrid operations, testing how EU states respond to disruption designed to sow fear.

left.angle: Left-leaning outlets led with the scale of disruption and tied it to the wider hybrid-warfare debate, also giving space to Italian opposition criticism of the government.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Covers Thursday's second wave, Meloni's no-evacuation guidance and opposition attacks on defence spending.

outlets.name: CNN
outlets.note: Evacuations in Italy and alarm in the UK and Ireland.

right.angle: Right-leaning US coverage stressed that authorities found no credible danger and leaned on officials' 'cyber attack' description, adding speculation about a bigger agenda without naming a culprit.

outlets.name: Townhall
outlets.note: Built around social-media posts and Italy's education minister calling it a cyber attack, not a real risk.

stories.differ: Left-leaning coverage frames it as a security and political story; right-leaning coverage frames it as a hoax and disruption story.
